records.sourceFile: The influence of injury history on countermovement jump performance and movement strategy in professional soccer players - Implications for prof.pdf

paper.citation: Mitchell A, Holding C, Greig M. The Influence of Injury History on Countermovement Jump Performance and Movement Strategy in Professional Soccer Players: Implications for Profiling and Rehabilitation Foci. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2021;30(5):768-773.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared 10 professional soccer players with a prior lower-limb injury and 10 without, using double-leg and single-leg jumps on force plates. Single-leg jump performance and movement strategy differed between the groups, while double-leg jump results did not, which the authors link to limb compensation.
paper.tldr: Single-leg countermovement jumps reveal deficits in players with a previous injury, while the usual double-leg jump does not. For profiling and rehabilitation, look at how the jump is produced, especially the eccentric phase, not only jump height.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional comparison of double-leg and single-leg countermovement jumps on force plates, with five trials per test. Injured players were matched to uninjured squad members on demographics, and group effects were tested with general linear models. Single-leg data pooled both limbs for each player, and hierarchical regression ordered the force variables that predicted jump performance.
paper.findings: Double-leg jump height and flight time to contraction time ratio did not differ between groups. In single-leg jumps, the previously injured group had lower jump height (p = 0.007) and flight time to contraction time ratio (p = 0.005), with lower eccentric and concentric peak force and rate of force development, and a deeper countermovement in the affected limb (22.3 vs 16.7 cm). The uninjured limb of injured players also performed below the uninjured group. In uninjured players, eccentric and concentric force variables explained most of the variation in performance, while in injured players only concentric variables did.
paper.limitations: Ten players per group from one club, with no baseline before injury and no detail on injury type or timing, and the cross-sectional design cannot show that injury caused the differences. Pooling both limbs per player is not independent, and the noninjured values in Table 3 (0.89 for jump height, 0.44 for time ratio) are reversed relative to the text (44% and 89%).
paper.practicalImplications: In squads with injury history, consider single-leg jumps alongside double-leg jumps, and record force-time variables such as peak force, rate of force development and eccentric phase, not just jump height. The authors suggest rehabilitation targeting eccentric force development in both limbs, and checking the uninjured limb too. Use the squad's own baselines to interpret any single-leg result.
paper.athleteDev: For squad profiling, a single-leg jump with force-plate variables may show movement differences that a double-leg jump hides. Interpret results against each player's own baseline, since these are group-level differences in 20 players.
paper.rtp: The paper argues that a player whose jump height looks normal can still have eccentric force deficits after injury, so jump height alone should not clear a player to return. It did not test return-to-play decisions or whether these deficits predict re-injury, so it cannot set clearance cut-offs.
